messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh Tran, a 35-year-old accountant, described the torture he endured in sparse, broken sections that rarely stayed in order for long. He had come to the United States from Southeast Asia as a young adult, and when he spoke about what happened, the account did not unfold as a single story so much as flashes that seized him: a locked room, voices he did not recognize, the shock of being cornered by men whose intentions he could not read until it was too late. Even in session, he would stop and frown as if the sequence kept slipping away. He knew certain moments with painful clarity, but he could not reliably say what came first and what followed. What was most striking was the way he spoke about the memory itself. At times he referred to the man in those scenes almost as if it were someone else, saying things in a detached way that made it sound as though the memory belonged to another person and not to him. Yet the images returned with relentless force, replaying like a film he had not chosen to watch, cutting into ordinary moments without warning.

In the months after the torture, Minh found that these scenes came to mind suddenly and with a vividness that made the present recede. He could be at his desk reviewing spreadsheets, the steady order of numbers on the screen briefly giving way to a flash from the room where he had been held, and for a moment he was no longer an accountant in an office but back inside that experience. Because the memories arrived abruptly, he became wary of situations that seemed to open the door to them. Conversations about the future were especially difficult. Colleagues would make casual remarks about next quarter, retirement planning, vacations, or where they saw themselves in five years, and Minh would go quiet or excuse himself. He could not explain it easily to others, but talk of the future felt unreal and destabilizing. It forced him up against the fact that there had been a time when he could not see beyond the next hour, and he now found himself unable to imagine a future without that history intruding.

Talking to strangers also became charged. During the torture, much of the fear had centered on not knowing who the men were, what they wanted, or what they would do next. Since then, unfamiliar people had come to feel dangerous precisely because they were unknown. Minh was certain that you could never really know who might harm you. In practice this meant small but narrowing changes in daily life. At work he began sending emails instead of walking over to speak with people he did not know well. If a new client came into the accounting office and tried to make light conversation, he kept his answers clipped and looked for a reason to leave. He avoided networking events entirely. Even routine encounters in the lobby or elevator could leave him tense and watchful, studying tone of voice, facial expression, and distance in a way that exhausted him by the end of the day.

Over time he also came to believe that what had happened had altered him permanently for the worse. He compared himself harshly to an imagined version of “somebody else” who, in his mind, would have stopped the event from happening. That belief was not presented as an abstract idea but as a private indictment he returned to again and again: another man would have seen it coming, reacted faster, found a way out. Minh spoke with evident shame when he said this, even while acknowledging that he had been overpowered. The divorce that followed in later years sat in his mind alongside these conclusions about himself, not as something he elaborated on in detail, but as further proof that he was no longer the person he had been meant to be.

By the time he sought help, his world had grown smaller and more rigid. His job as an accountant still suited the part of him that wanted predictability, but even there he felt cornered by sudden memory intrusions and by the ordinary social demands of office life. The immediate reason he came to treatment was a recent meeting in which a discussion about long-term planning led him to dissociate into one of the film-like replays so intensely that he lost track of the conversation and had to leave the room. He was frightened by how quickly it happened and by how little control he seemed to have over it. What he feared most was that this was final—that he had been changed beyond repair and would spend the rest of his life bracing against strangers, against the future, and against a memory that did not feel fully like his own. What he hoped for, cautiously, was not to erase what happened, but to be able to remain in the present when it came back.
